newsitem.title: SWEDEN: TENNIS-GENTLEMAN EDBERG BOWS OUT WITH A LIMP.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GENTLEMAN EDBERG BOWS OUT WITH A LIMP.

text.p: Stefan Edberg, the gentleman Swede, retired from competitive tennis on Sunday, forced to pull out of his last Davis Cup final match because of a twisted ankle.
It was an unfitting farewell for the 30-year-old right-hander, who would have liked to have given his home fans something to cheer during a last appearance against the French challengers.

Edberg, who announced a year ago that he would retire at the end of 1996, fell heavily in the opening singles against Cedric Pioline and his wrenched ankle could not recover in time for the reverse match against Arnaud Boetsch.
Edberg's 14-year professional career coincided with a boom in tennis as more money was poured into the game and prizes grew.

But the gentle, softly spoken Swede never let the pressure get to him on court. While opponents such as John McEnroe or Jimmy Connors might rant and rave at mistakes or disputed line-calls, Edberg would merely shake his blond head and get on with the game.
His courteous behaviour earned him the admiration and respect of players and spectators alike.
"We all have huge respect for Stefan -- the way he acts, the way he plays he has been a role model," Yannick Noah, France's Davis Cup captain and a frequest Edberg adversary said during the final.
Edberg's first tournament title was in Milan in 1984 at the age of 18 after he was disccovered by Percy Rosberg, who coached compatriot Bjorn Borg.
He went from strength to strength, playing more than 1,000 matches and winning 41 singles and 18 doubles titles as well as helping Sweden to four Davis Cups. He earned some $20.7 million.
A consummate serve-and-volleyer, Edberg was happy on grass, winning Wimbledon twice in 1988 and 1990. He also made his home in London, a stone's throw from the Queen's Club.
He won the Australian Open in 1985 and 1987 and the doubles title there in 1987 and again this year with Petr Korda.
Then he captured the U.S. Open title in 1991 and 1992 after winning the doubles there in 1987.

Only the French Open, played on the slow clay he felt least at home with, eluded him, though he reached the final in 1989. Touchingly, it was Roland Garros that gave him one of the warmest ovations of his farewell year.

Afterwards the measured Swede almost succumbed to emotion. "It's hard sometimes to come up with the words," he said. "I think I've shown the crowd by playing tennis and they've shown their appreciation by giving me a bit of an ovation after the match."
Edberg spent a total of 72 weeks ranked number one in the world, finishing 1990 and 1991 at the top, and he stayed in the top 10 for 10 years.
Although he could still produce some brilliant touches and is currently ranked a very respectable 14, Edberg's form began to slip in the mid 1990s.

"I had seen other top players fading away and I think I owe it to myself not to do that," he said. "And I think you have other values once you start a family. You find there are other things in life."
Edberg and his wife Annette have a three-year-old daughter Emilie.

The family may move back to Sweden where Edberg has set up a foundation to help aspiring new players. He will spend some time with that, but says he does not want to take up coaching until later in life. A break from the game, he feels, would do him good.

He will decide what to do with his life after a little holdiay. "A few months off will be next for me," he said after his final tournament in Stockholm last month. "I will have time over Christmas and New Year and will think about what I want to do."
